The person is saying that they've been eating a lot of potato chips, and because of that, they feel justified in expecting a lecture from their mailman. Wait, why would the mailman lecture them about eating potato chips? Mailmen are supposed to deliver mail, right? They're not health professionals or anything like that. Maybe the person is thinking that the mailman sees them every day and notices that they're eating unhealthy snacks. So, they assume that the mailman would have an opinion on their eating habits and would feel the need to lecture them. But is that a reasonable expectation? I guess it depends on the relationship between the person and the mailman. If they have a close relationship where they talk about personal things, maybe the mailman could offer some advice. But generally, mailmen are just there to deliver mail. They don't have a responsibility to monitor people's eating habits or give them advice on diet. Also, expecting a lecture from someone who isn't in a position to give advice might come off as presumptuous. It's one thing to receive unsolicited advice, but expecting it might set up unrealistic expectations. Plus, it could potentially strain the relationship if the mailman feels uncomfortable or doesn't want to engage in that kind of conversation. Another angle to consider is the person's own responsibility for their health. If they're concerned about eating too many potato chips, it might be more productive to take steps themselves, like reducing their intake or talking to a healthcare professional, rather than expecting someone else to intervene. So, putting it all together, expecting a lecture from the mailman about eating potato chips seems a bit unreasonable. The mailman's role is to deliver mail, not to provide dietary advice. It might be better for the person to take personal responsibility for their health rather than expecting others to lecture them.
